source.title: NeuronGuard: Robust LLM Safety Alignment via Ablation-Aware Safety Signal Redistribution
source.authors: Anjun Gao; Yueyang Quan; Yufei Xia; Zhuqing Liu; Minghong Fang

record.file_problem: None noted; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports attack-success rates for adversarial suffix and neuron-pruning attacks, testing whether these attacks bypass safety behavior. It does not reproduce the cited fine-tuning or per-token KL measurements.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own GCG suffix-attack and NeuroStrike neuron-pruning ASR results, including the no-defense and NeuronGuard conditions across reported utility tasks, plus the adaptive pruning attacks. The paper's statements about prior work finding sparse safety neurons are cited background, not rows. Its refusal-training objective and claims about redistributing signals are not standalone outcome rows. It does not test harmful or benign fine-tuning as a cause of refusal loss, token-position KL concentration, prefilling, decoding changes, or why safety is shallow.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a defense paper, but it reports attack success rates (ASR) for existing attacks on undefended models. These are Llama/Qwen/Falcon instruct models after benign LoRA fine-tuning. GCG suffix ASR bears on V4 and targeted neuron-pruning ASR (NeuroStrike, IP, NE) bears on V5. NeuronGuard results are the study's own method and do not measure any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors claim NeuronGuard redistributes safety across neurons and gives near-zero ASR against jailbreak and neuron-pruning attacks, including multimodal and white-box adaptive settings, while keeping task accuracy. They frame sparse safety neurons as the root cause of fragility.
record.recipe_differences: This paper trains a defense using refusal losses under normal and neuron-ablated passes, KL consistency regularization, and randomized gradient projection, then evaluates attack ASR. It does not apply the original studies' harmful/benign fine-tuning intervention or measure per-token KL concentration.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR varies with utility task, attack type, model, and defense condition. In the Llama SST2 analysis, ASR also changes with the neuron masking fraction ρ, classifier refresh interval N, probe-set size, and static versus dynamic neuron identification (Sections 6–7 and Tables 6–13); these analyses concern NeuronGuard's defense performance, not the first-token claim.

fits_no_version.finding: Training with ablation of identified safety neurons (NeuronGuard) cuts NeuroStrike ASR from 0.81–0.91 to 0.00–0.04, and IP/NE ASR to 0.09/0.05. GCG ASR falls to ≤0.03.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron-level redistribution training removes the localization of safety, as a parameter-space analogue of deepening.

record.problems: ASR is reported as averages over 10 random seeds, but no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or p-values are given. The reported attack results do not directly quantify the fraction of weights or neurons carrying safety, and the paper reports no random-neuron-pruning comparison. The claims about token-position concentration are not measured.
record.rows_left_out: Other jailbreak attacks (PAIR, TAP, Puzzler, AutoDAN) were not included because the versions tested here specifically concern adversarial suffixes and neuron-level localization/pruning. Other defense-baseline results were omitted because they do not add a distinct result about those claim objects. The ablation-ratio, refresh-interval, probe-size, and component-variant tables evaluate NeuronGuard design choices rather than token-depth or fine-tuning-induced refusal loss.

untested.parts: Models are benign LoRA-fine-tuned, but no pre- vs post-fine-tuning harmful compliance is reported.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
The fraction of neurons NeuroStrike prunes is not reported here, and there is no random-pruning control. Weights and ranks are not examined.
No test of what data or objective causes shallowness.
No token-depth training. NeuronGuard spreads safety across neurons, not response positions.

missing.what: Variant I (refusal training only, no ablation) still has NeuroStrike ASR 0.71. This shows plain refusal training leaves safety prunable.
Undefended Qwen2.5-VL-7B under NeuroStrike: ASR 0.99 (StrongREJECT T2I) and 0.96 (NSFW).
SafeNeuron (freezing-based redistribution) leaves NeuroStrike ASR at 0.21–0.28, and static identification at 0.29.

record.verdict_notes: The undefended baselines are already LoRA-fine-tuned on benign tasks, and no pre-fine-tuning or no-attack ASR is given. These baselines therefore cannot isolate V2 or show V4's effect over baseline. ASR is judged by Llama-Guard-3-8B on StrongREJECT. No variance is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment fine-tunes safety-trained models on harmful examples to measure loss of refusal.
No experiment tests ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning data for harmful compliance.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Tests GCG adversarial suffixes, but not compliant-token prefilling or decoding changes.

Tests targeted neuron-pruning attacks and resulting ASR, but does not directly quantify how much safety is carried by a small set of weights or ranks, nor compare targeted pruning with random pruning.
Does not test whether particular data or training objectives produce first-token shallowness.
Trains a defense intended to redistribute safety signals, but does not measure safety depth across response-token positions or test whether safety is spread beyond the first tokens.
